extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in transition-to-advanced-math, instructors, and self-guided graduate students (Statistics, CS, Physics, Engineering, Finance, Economics, Business)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance for learning how to read, understand, and construct mathematical proofs, including specific proof techniques and higher-level mathematical thinking processes. Suitable as a textbook for a transition-to-proof course, course supplement, or self-study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and description of proof techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: The various techniques used in virtually all proofs, independent of subject matter, are identified and described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part 1 of the book catalogs techniques used in proofs so students can learn a toolbox of methods applicable across subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use each technique (keyword-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are taught not only how to use the techniques, but also when each technique is likely to be used, based on certain keywords that appear in the statement under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes recognizing linguistic cues in problem statements that suggest particular methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding written proofs by identifying sequence of techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are taught how to understand a written proof by learning to identify the sequence of techniques that are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on reverse-engineering proofs: spotting the methods applied and their order to follow logical flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-Backward Method
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a general proof technique; included among core methods students should learn to apply and recognize.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Definitions and Mathematical Terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of definitions and mathematical terminology (chapter 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers the role of precise definitions and language in constructing and understanding proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers I: The Construction Method
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique for existential/constructive proofs: how to construct an example to satisfy existence statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers II: The Choose Method
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique for handling quantifiers by choosing appropriate elements; guidance on how to make choices in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers III: Specialization
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using specialization of general statements/variables to derive consequences or simplify arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers IV: Nested Quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques for reasoning with multiple, nested quantifiers and their logical order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nots of Nots Lead to Knots (negation techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nots of Nots Lead to Knots (chapter 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handling negation and double-negation in statements and proofs; avoids common pitfalls with 'not' structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Contradiction Method
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using indirect proof by assuming the negation and deriving a contradiction; when and how to apply it.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Contrapositive Method
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving implications by proving the contrapositive; guidance on recognizing when contrapositive is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness Methods
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques for proving uniqueness statements (show existence and then show any two solutions must coincide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of mathematical induction and variants; covers structure of base case and inductive step and common induction pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either/Or (case analysis)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handling proofs that require case splits; organizing arguments by exhaustive cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Max/Min Methods
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques using extremal principles (choose maximal or minimal elements) to drive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization (mathematical thinking)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes and illustrates how to generalize results and spot patterns extending specific cases to broader contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating Mathematical Definitions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on how to form useful, precise definitions and the role of definitions in proofs and theory-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic Systems / Abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiomatic Systems and Abstraction (Part 2, chapter 18 and listed items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses abstraction and axiomatics: building theories from axioms and understanding their logical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion/illustration of unifying disparate results or concepts under a common framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting visual images to symbolic form and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting visual images to symbolic form and vice versa (Part 2 list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques for translating diagrams/visual intuition into formal symbolic proofs and for using visual reasoning effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cross-subject examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendices provide examples of proofs from Discrete Mathematics, Linear Algebra, Modern Algebra, and Real Analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposes students to how techniques apply across different mathematical areas; supports transfer of skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solutions to Selected Exercises
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides worked solutions to help students check understanding and learn proof-writing by example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia lecture support
rubrics_metrics.description: Videos of lectures for each of the first 15 chapters are available (linked resource).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementary lectures accompany chapters to reinforce techniques and provide guided instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended course uses and audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is suitable as a text for an undergraduate transition-to-advanced-math course, as a supplement to any course involving proofs, or for self-guided reading (especially for Ph.D. students in math-related areas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies target instructional contexts and broader audiences who will benefit from the material.
